newsitem.title: USA: Vitamin E, Parkinson drug may slow Alzheimers - study.
newsitem.headline: Vitamin E, Parkinson drug may slow Alzheimers - study.

text.p: Vitamin E and a drug used to treat Parkinson's disease may slow the deterioration caused by Alzheimer's disease, researchers reported on Wednesday.
Both substances are already available to the public, and scientists said there is likely to be an immediate impact on treatment.

"I think it's a big deal for two reasons," Mary Sano of Columbia University's College of Physicians and Surgeons said at a news conference. "These are outcomes that relate to the quality of life of patients and their families ... The second reason is because it's important to do these kinds of ... long studies and look at meaningful outcomes."

The study found that both Vitamin E and the anti-Parkinson's drug selegiline appeared to delay for six to seven months the milestones of the disease, such as required institutionalization, inability to perform basic activities of living, severe dementia and death.
Sano led a team that followed 341 patients with moderately severe Alzheimer's symptoms over two years.

The patients were divided into four groups, with one group getting a placebo, another getting 10 mg daily of selegiline, a third getting 2,000 international units (about 2,000 mg) of Vitamin E -- four to five times the normal daily dose -- and a fourth group getting a combination of Vitamin E and selegiline.

The placebo group lagged behind the other three. The other three groups were statistically similar in slowing the effects of Alzheimer's, the researchers said. The combination group did not show a notable advantage, the study found.

Findings were reported in Wednesday's New England Journal of Medicine, and one scientist who worked on the study, Dr. Leon Thal of the University of California, San Diego, said patients would be lining up to buy Vitamin E by Thursday morning. "It's cheap, too," he said.

Thal and Sano stressed that their study only looked at patients with moderately severe symptoms, not those without symptoms or those with severe symptoms. They noted that neither Vitamin E nor selegiline brought improvement in Alzheimer's patients, only a slowing of deterioration.
Selegiline is sold under the brand name Eldepryl by Somerset Pharmaceuticals.

Both selegiline and high doses of Vitamin E carry potential problems. Selegiline should not be taken with certain anti-depressants and narcotics, and Vitamin E may increase the risk of bleeding problems in some people, the researchers said.

Edward Truschke, president of the Alzheimer's Association, which provides support and research funds to combat the disease, hailed the study's results in a statement: "We are very excited that the study showed not only that the clinical signs of disease progression can be slowed but also that, for the first time, drugs were effective with people in the moderately severe stages of the disease."

The study drew words of caution in an editorial in the New England Journal of Medicine from two experts who warn that quirks in the way the study was done may give a false impression that the treatments seem to work.
Further tests will be needed to discover whether the research represents real progress against a disease that affects up to 30 percent of people over age 85.
